title: Any Reference To%20acts%207 Verse 39 And 40 Further Biblical Explanation
paragraphs: Understanding Acts 7:39-40—Israel’s Rejection of Moses

The seventh chapter of Acts records Stephen’s defense before the Sanhedrin, where he recounts Israel’s history to highlight their persistent resistance to God’s messengers. In Acts 7:39 and Acts 7:40, Stephen addresses a pivotal moment of rebellion in Israel’s wilderness journey.
to whom our fathers would not be obedient, but thrust him from them, and turned back in their hearts unto Egypt, - Acts 7:39 ASV
saying unto Aaron, Make us gods that shall go before us: for as for this Moses, who led us forth out of the land of Egypt, we know not what is become of him. - Acts 7:40 ASV
The Context: Stephen’s Appeal to Israel’s History

Stephen’s purpose is to show that Israel’s rejection of Jesus is consistent with their past. By referencing the golden calf incident (Exodus 32:1), he emphasizes the people’s tendency to turn from God’s appointed deliverers and return to idolatry.
Key Biblical Themes in Acts 7:39-40
1. Rebellion Against God’s Appointed Leader
Moses was chosen by God to lead Israel out of Egypt, yet the people rejected him:
And they said one to another, Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt. - Numbers 14:4 ASV
This rebellion is not just against Moses but against God Himself, who raised Moses as their deliverer (Exodus 3:10).
2. The Heart’s Turn Toward Egypt

Despite witnessing God’s mighty acts, the Israelites’ hearts “turned back” to Egypt. Egypt often symbolizes bondage and sin in Scripture. Their longing for Egypt represented a desire to return to their old way of life, rather than embrace God’s promises.
But lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, And tempted God in the desert. - Psalm 106:14 ASV
3. The Sin of Idolatry

Israel’s demand for “gods that shall go before us” reveals a deeper spiritual problem: a lack of trust in God’s presence and provision. Their impatience and unbelief led to idolatry, a recurring issue in Israel’s history.
They made a calf in Horeb, And worshipped a molten image. - Psalm 106:19 ASV
Scripture consistently warns against idolatry as a betrayal of the living God (Exodus 20:3; 1 Corinthians 10:7).
Theological Insights
Sinful Repetition: Stephen’s message is that history repeats itself—God’s people have consistently resisted His revelation and chosen their own way.
Christ as the Greater Moses: Just as Israel rejected Moses, many rejected Christ, the ultimate Deliverer (John 1:11). Yet, salvation is available to all who trust in Him by faith (Romans 10:9).
Warning for Believers: The call is to guard our hearts against unbelief and idolatry, fixing our eyes on Jesus and trusting God’s promises (Hebrews 3:12).
Application for Today

These verses challenge believers to examine their own hearts. Are there areas where we are tempted to “turn back” to old patterns or idols rather than trust God’s leading? The gospel offers hope and transformation through faith in Christ, who delivers us from the bondage of sin to walk in newness of life (2 Corinthians 5:17).
